source.title: PII Jailbreaking in LLMs via Activation Steering Reveals Personal Information Leakage
source.authors: K. K. Nakka; Xue Jiang; Dmitrii Usynin; Xue-Bing Zhou

record.tranche_reason: The study uses attention-head activation steering as a privacy-jailbreaking attack and reports its performance. It does not test the specific difference-in-means refusal direction or the versions of the claim.
record.gate_note: The intervention adds probe-trained vectors to selected attention heads at the last input token; it does not ablate or add the claimed single difference-in-means direction. The study reports probe predictiveness and privacy-jailbreaking outcomes. Hyperparameter-specific counts in Figure 6 are not extracted here because they are shown only in the plot.
record.test_reason: The study trains ridge-regression probes on attention-head activations to separate privacy refusals from disclosures. It then adds scaled probe weights to the top-k heads at the last prompt token to induce disclosure, and reports only this attack's success and factuality rates. It never computes a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, never ablates a direction across layers and positions, and never edits weights. It does not check other capabilities, compare single versus multiple directions, or cite the original. The target behaviour is privacy refusal on one attribute, not refusal of harmful instructions. The result is a cousin of V1 (linear steering can flip refusal) but does not test any version as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that steering probe-selected attention heads bypasses privacy refusals and can elicit factual memorised personal information, a privacy risk warranting stronger testing.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains linear probes to distinguish privacy responses and adds their learned vectors to selected attention heads at the last input token. It does not use a harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation direction or project a direction out across layers and positions.
record.method_sensitivity: Disclosure outcomes vary with steering strength and the number of selected heads; the authors state that effective parameter combinations occupy a smaller region and that the optimal combination varies across models.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-head linear probes on last-token attention activations predict privacy refusal vs disclosure. The best Llama2-7B probe reaches AUC 0.89 and F1 0.83, with middle layers most predictive.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Privacy-refusal decisions are linearly decodable from attention-head activations at the prompt's last token.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding negatively scaled probe weights to top-k heads yields at least one disclosure in 66 configurations for 80–96% of non-disclosing subjects across three models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Probe-direction steering of a few attention heads can bypass privacy refusals.

fits_no_version.finding: 68.8–89.9% of jailbroken subjects had at least one response judged factual by GPT-4o-mini. Manual checks covered only 10 subjects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering-induced privacy disclosures can contain real memorised personal information.

fits_no_version.finding: Baseline disclosure on a sexual-orientation query ranges from 1.5% to 84% across seven open models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Privacy alignment differs widely across model providers and versions.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 6th Workshop on Trustworthy NLP (TrustNLP 2026)
record.problems: Factuality rates rely first on an LLM evaluator; manual verification is limited to 10 subjects. The authors also report human-annotator disagreement for disclosure labels. Table and prose differ slightly for the Qwen jailbreak rate, and model-size labels for GLM are inconsistent across sections and tables.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 6 shows parameter-specific disclosure counts across steering strengths and head counts, but the plot-only values are not transcribed into separate condition rows here. Probe results for other models are plotted in Figures 5 and 7 without corresponding exact values in the text.

untested.parts: Difference-in-means direction; directional ablation removing refusal; adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts; capability preservation. The study's probe-weight steering on privacy refusal is related but not this test.
No analysis of whether jailbreaks suppress a refusal direction; no adversarial training.
No comparison of single versus multiple or affine directions.
Harmfulness judgment is not separated from the refusal decision.
No transfer across languages, models or base/instruct versions.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T4/uses_without_test call is reasonable. One could argue T6, since the paper does not cite Arditi et al. and relies on head-level probe steering (Kim et al. 2025) rather than the refusal direction. Negative alpha drives disclosure because the probe is trained with refused=1, so subtracting the 'refusal' probe direction is loosely analogous to direction removal. However, this is additive steering on a few heads, not projection ablation, and there are no controls or capability checks.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test the difference-in-means direction, removal across layers and positions, adding that direction to induce refusals, or preservation of general capability.
No weight edit or abliteration is tested.
The attack does not test whether attacks suppress the claimed direction, and no training against its ablation is performed.
The study does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account of refusal.
The study does not separate harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or direction-transfer test is reported.
The study does not vary refusal training methods or stages.
